journeys.title: BOQ events
journeys.goal: Create and publish a bill-of-quantities event with its own line-item rules.

cases.title: Uploading a filled BOQ sheet creates one line item per row
cases.why: It is the core BOQ mechanic and the only bulk line-item path.
cases.setup: A filled sheet with 25 rows.
cases.steps: Upload it.
cases.expected: 25 line items, values as in the sheet.
cases.oracle: Badge = 25; spot-check three rows' product, quantity and unit.

cases.title: A BOQ project creates its draft event group exactly once on mount
cases.why: A re-render that fires it again produces two draft events and the buyer works in one while the other lingers.
cases.setup: gate: `boq_in_erfx_allowed`.
cases.steps: Enter BOQ project creation. Let the screen re-render (resize, switch tabs).
cases.expected: One draft event group.
cases.oracle: Exactly one create request; one draft in the events list.

cases.title: A BOQ event is accepted with no line items in the create request
cases.why: It is the one legal way to create an event with an empty `line_items` array — the flag is what makes it legal.
cases.setup: gate: `boq_in_erfx_allowed`.
cases.steps: Create the BOQ draft before uploading anything.
cases.expected: Created.
cases.oracle: Draft created with zero line items. Pairs with API-EG-004.

cases.title: BOQ creation is refused on a tenant that does not allow it
cases.why: The negative half of the gate; without it the flag is unproven.
cases.setup: A tenant without `boq_in_erfx_allowed`.
cases.steps: Attempt BOQ creation.
cases.expected: Refused ("You are not allowed to perform this action") or the entry point absent.
cases.oracle: No draft created. Pairs with API-EG-005.

cases.title: Downloading the blank BOQ template gives a usable sheet
cases.why: It is the buyer's starting point; a template whose columns do not match the importer is an immediate dead end.
cases.setup: A BOQ project with a template chosen.
cases.steps: Download the blank BOQ items sheet.
cases.expected: A spreadsheet whose columns match the chosen template's schema.
cases.oracle: Column headers equal the template's widget names.

cases.title: A malformed BOQ row is reported with its row number
cases.why: "Upload failed" on a 500-row sheet is useless; the row number is the whole value of the error.
cases.setup: A sheet with a bad quantity on row 12.
cases.steps: Upload.
cases.expected: A readable error naming row 12; either nothing imports or the good rows import and the bad one is listed.
cases.oracle: The message contains the row identifier; no 500.

cases.title: A BOQ upload with a product that does not exist is refused
cases.why: The backend answers "Product not found" (80) and the buyer needs to know which product.
cases.setup: A sheet naming an unknown product.
cases.steps: Upload.
cases.expected: Refused, naming the offending value.
cases.oracle: Message identifies the product; no partial import of that row.

cases.title: Re-uploading replaces the previous BOQ items
cases.why: Appending instead of replacing silently doubles a 500-row event.
cases.setup: A BOQ event with 25 items.
cases.steps: Upload a different 25-row sheet.
cases.expected: 25 items, the new ones; the old ones are removed.
cases.oracle: Count is 25, not 50; the old products are gone. Pairs with API-LI-007.

cases.title: 500 BOQ items publish
cases.why: The documented ceiling, and the only case that exercises the publish path at scale.
cases.setup: gate: `boq_in_erfx_allowed`.
cases.steps: Load 500 items. Publish.
cases.expected: Publishes.
cases.oracle: Publish succeeds; record the duration (see UI-NFR-004).

cases.title: A vendor bidding on a BOQ event gets all rows in their sheet
cases.why: A truncated vendor sheet produces a partial bid that looks complete.
cases.setup: A live BOQ event with 25 items and an invited vendor.
cases.steps: As the vendor, open the bid sheet.
cases.expected: 25 rows, matching the buyer's items.
cases.oracle: Row count and the products in each row match.

cases.title: 501 BOQ items are refused
cases.why: The other side of the boundary.
cases.steps: Attempt 501.
cases.expected: Refused with the max-line-items message.
cases.oracle: Message shown; the event keeps 500.

cases.title: A BOQ event linked to a purchase request validates the PR
cases.why: `purchase_request_id` must resolve to an active BOQ PR owned by the workspace, or the event is attached to nothing.
cases.setup: A BOQ project and an inactive/foreign PR id.
cases.steps: Attempt to link it.
cases.expected: Refused ("not allowed").
cases.oracle: No link created. Pairs with API-PUB-016.

journeys.title: From purchase request to event
journeys.goal: Turn an approved purchase requisition into a sourcing event.

cases.title: An approved PR converts into a draft event
cases.why: It is the intake-to-sourcing handoff, and everything about the resulting event is constrained by it.
cases.setup: gate: PR module. An approved PR with line items.
cases.steps: From the PR, create an event.
cases.expected: A draft event carrying the PR's line items and quantities.
cases.oracle: Line-item count and products match the PR; the event records the PR link.

cases.title: PR line items cannot be added to or removed
cases.why: Diverging from the requisition breaks the consumption reconciliation.
cases.setup: A PR-created draft.
cases.steps: Open the line-items drawer and try to add and remove.
cases.expected: Both inert.
cases.oracle: Controls disabled; count unchanged.

cases.title: PR quantities can be reduced and reconcile back
cases.why: Buyers routinely source part of a requisition; the remainder must return to the PR.
cases.setup: A PR line item of 100.
cases.steps: Reduce to 60 on the event. Publish. Open the PR.
cases.expected: The PR shows 60 in progress and 40 still open.
cases.oracle: PR in-progress quantity = 60. `update_quantity_of_purchase_request_items` is the mechanism.

cases.title: A quantity above the PR's is refused
cases.why: Sourcing more than was requisitioned is an approval bypass.
cases.setup: A PR line item of 100.
cases.steps: Set 150 on the event.
cases.expected: Refused with a readable message.
cases.oracle: Refusal; the PR is unchanged.

cases.title: A dormant-locked PR line item blocks creation before anything is written
cases.why: It has a dedicated error shape (not the generic `render_error_json`), and the guard runs before any write — so a partial event must never appear.
cases.setup: A PR whose line item is dormant-locked.
cases.steps: Try to create an event from it.
cases.expected: Refused with the dormant-PR message; no draft created.
cases.oracle: Zero drafts for that PR afterwards. Pairs with API-EG-006.

cases.title: Awarding a PR-created event writes back to the PR
cases.why: It closes the intake loop; without it the PR stays open forever.
cases.setup: A PR-created event, awarded.
cases.steps: Complete the award. Open the PR.
cases.expected: The PR reflects the awarded quantity and vendor.
cases.oracle: PR state and awarded quantity match the proposal.

cases.title: Withdrawing a PR-created event returns the quantity to the PR
cases.why: Otherwise a withdrawn event permanently consumes the requisition.
cases.setup: A published PR-created event.
cases.steps: Withdraw it. Open the PR.
cases.expected: The in-progress quantity returns to open.
cases.oracle: PR open quantity is back to its pre-event value.

cases.title: A PR-created event cannot be cloned
cases.why: Already stated as UI-PUB-022; here it is reached from the PR side, which is how a buyer actually meets it.
cases.setup: A published PR-created event.
cases.steps: Try to clone.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Message shown.

cases.title: Multiple PRs merged into one event keep their PR numbers per row
cases.why: The PR-number column is how the buyer proves which requisition a row served.
cases.setup: Two approved PRs.
cases.steps: Create one event from both.
cases.expected: Every line item shows its originating PR number.
cases.oracle: Each row's `pr_number` matches its source PR.

cases.title: A PR-created event's line item cannot be deleted below one
cases.why: Combines the PR constraint with the 711 rule; the message must be the readable one, not a raw code.
cases.setup: A PR-created event with one line item.
cases.steps: Try to delete it.
cases.expected: Refused with "You cannot delete this line item from the project".
cases.oracle: Message shown; item remains.

journeys.title: Classic single-stage events
journeys.goal: Use the non-eRFX single-stage screen, where the event type is chosen in a drawer.

cases.title: A single-stage RFQ publishes
cases.why: The most reliable event in the product and the seed for §15 and §16.
cases.setup: Buyer with trade create; single-stage entry.
cases.steps: Create → configure `eventType: rfq`, `awarding: lot` → title → Buy template → fill the first line item → add a participant → Publish.
cases.expected: Lands on `/project/:id/details` with the event Live.
cases.oracle: A real project id in the URL; no error toast.

cases.title: A single-stage RFP publishes
cases.why: The classic path has its own RFP shape, distinct from eRFX's technical stage.
cases.steps: As UI-SS-001 with `eventType: rfp`.
cases.expected: Publishes.
cases.oracle: Project id; the event type reads RFP.

cases.title: A single-stage auction publishes with each sub-type
cases.why: Rank, price and traffic light are all selectable here, and the sub-type section only renders after the event type is chosen — a timing trap.
cases.steps: For each of rank / price / traffic light: configure and publish.
cases.expected: All three publish with the chosen sub-type.
cases.oracle: Sub-type on the live event matches; wait for the conditional section to render before selecting.

cases.title: The configuration drawer renders awarding only after event type
cases.why: Selecting awarding before the type finds nothing and the run reports a missing control.
cases.setup: A fresh single-stage create.
cases.steps: Open the drawer and observe which sections exist before and after choosing a type.
cases.expected: Sub-type and awarding appear only after the type is chosen.
cases.oracle: Options absent before, present after.

cases.title: Awarding "entire lot to a single vendor" is honoured downstream
cases.why: It constrains the awarding grid, so a mismatch surfaces only at award time.
cases.steps: Publish lot-based; reach the awarding screen.
cases.expected: The grid allows one winner for the whole lot.
cases.oracle: Awarding mode reads lot at both ends.

cases.title: Awarding "partially award to multiple vendors" is honoured downstream
cases.why: The other mode, and the one the two-competing-bids journey needs.
cases.steps: Publish line-item based; reach the awarding screen.
cases.expected: Per-line allocation across vendors.
cases.oracle: Awarding mode reads line_item at both ends.

cases.title: Line items are the template's sheet rows
cases.why: It is the structural difference from eRFX, and the reason the eRFX line-item helper does not work here.
cases.setup: A single-stage create with a Buy template.
cases.steps: Fill the first row's product, variant, quantity, delivery and price cells.
cases.expected: One line item exists, defined by that row.
cases.oracle: The row is complete and the event publishes with one item.

cases.title: Publishing with an incomplete row is refused
cases.why: The sheet is the line items here, so a half row is a half event.
cases.steps: Leave the delivery location blank and publish.
cases.expected: Refused with a readable message.
cases.oracle: Publish blocked; no 500.

cases.title: "Invite whole audience" is the fallback when a named vendor is not found
cases.why: It is what keeps the bid journey alive on a tenant where the named test vendor is not in the searchable list — but it must be reported, because the run is then bidding as *someone*, not as the intended vendor.
cases.setup: A vendor search term that matches nothing.
cases.steps: Search, fail, fall back to inviting the audience, publish.
cases.expected: The event publishes with a non-zero audience.
cases.oracle: Audience count > 0 **and** a log line saying the named vendor was not matched. Never assert the specific vendor is on the event after this fallback.

cases.title: Scheduling a single-stage event for later works
cases.why: It was thought broken for a long time; the real cause was that the Schedule control is disabled until a line item exists ("Please choose a template and add a product").
cases.setup: A single-stage create with a template and one line item.
cases.steps: Open Schedule Event, set start/end and evaluation duration, Save Schedule.
cases.expected: The drawer opens and the schedule persists.
cases.oracle: Reopened drawer shows the saved window.

cases.title: A classic event's detail page exposes the same lifecycle controls
cases.why: §15 to §17 navigate from here; if the tabs differ, the later cases need a different path.
cases.setup: A published single-stage event.
cases.steps: Read the tab strip and the Settings menu.
cases.expected: Participants, bids/comparison, Master QCS and Settings are reachable.
cases.oracle: Each entry point resolves.

cases.title: A single-stage event is unaffected by eRFX-only gates
cases.why: It is why this path survived the activation regression, and it is worth an explicit assertion so the isolation is not accidental.
cases.setup: A tenant where eRFX publish is failing.
cases.steps: Publish a single-stage event.
cases.expected: Succeeds.
cases.oracle: Publish succeeds while the eRFX path fails — report both in one run so the contrast is visible.

cases.title: Stage tabs do not appear on a classic tenant
cases.why: The clearest structural assertion that the right screen is under test — the "wrong screen" mistake is the most expensive one in this catalog.
cases.setup: A tenant with `rfx_project_enabled` off.
cases.steps: Open the create screen.
cases.expected: No stage tab strip, no `+` stage control anywhere.
cases.oracle: Zero elements matching the tab strip.

cases.title: Adding a second sheet row adds a second line item
cases.why: Multi-line classic events behave differently from eRFX's shared project items.
cases.steps: Add a second row and publish.
cases.expected: Two line items on the live event.
cases.oracle: Line-item count = 2.

journeys.title: The event's lifecycle
journeys.goal: Manage an event after publish — extend, close, withdraw — and see it move Live → History.

cases.expected: The app accepts the request and answers with a success.

cases.title: Withdrawing an active event requires a remark and succeeds
cases.why: It is the buyer's emergency stop, and the remark is the audit trail vendors are shown.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "withdrawn"` and `withdraw_remark: {remarks, attachments}`.
cases.expected: 200; status withdrawn.
cases.oracle: Status withdrawn and the remark stored. ≈ BE-2.17.

cases.title: Activating a withdrawn event is refused
cases.why: Resurrecting a withdrawn event reopens bidding vendors were told was over.
cases.steps: `PATCH` a withdrawn event with `status: "active"`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Status stays withdrawn. ≈ BE-9.1.

cases.section: Issue a new version of the event — `POST /item_versions`
cases.title: Issue a new version of the event returns readable data

cases.setup: A buyer walking the API journey (RFQ only), at the step "Issue a new version of the event".

cases.expected: The app answers with structured data (JSON), not an error page or blank reply.
cases.oracle: Checked automatically on every API journey run; the report shows what actually came back. Engine check: `json_body`, learned from 4 real response(s).

cases.title: The new version's round ids is not empty
cases.why: It carried items in every real response; an empty list here means the thing just created or requested went missing.
cases.setup: A buyer walking the API journey (RFQ only), at the step "Issue a new version of the event".

cases.oracle: Checked automatically on every API journey run; the report shows what actually came back. Engine check: `non_empty new_item_data.trade_uuids`, learned from 4 real response(s).

cases.title: The new version of the event's new version's details is returned

cases.title: The new version of the event's new version's details is a set of details

cases.title: Withdrawing with blank remarks is refused
cases.why: Without it, an event can vanish for vendors with no explanation.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "withdrawn"` and empty remarks.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Status unchanged. ≈ BE-2.18.

cases.title: Withdrawal notifies vendors exactly once
cases.why: The mail fires on the status transition; two mails is a support call and none leaves vendors bidding on a dead event.
cases.steps: Withdraw, then re-issue the withdrawal.
cases.expected: One notification overall.
cases.oracle: Count the enqueued mail jobs across both calls. ≈ BE-9.2.

cases.title: Withdrawing twice is idempotent
cases.why: Retries happen; a second withdrawal record would corrupt the history.
cases.steps: `PATCH` withdrawn twice.
cases.expected: One withdrawal.
cases.oracle: One remark, one status change.

cases.title: Withdrawal releases the PR's in-progress quantity
cases.why: `update_in_progress_quantity` fires on the withdrawn transition; without it a withdrawn event permanently consumes the requisition.
cases.setup: A PR-linked published event.
cases.steps: Withdraw it. Read the PR.
cases.expected: The quantity returns to open.
cases.oracle: PR open quantity back to its pre-event value.

cases.title: An active event can be cloned
cases.why: It is how buyers run a recurring event, and its policy has four separate refusal conditions.
cases.steps: `POST /event_groups/:uuid/create_clone`.
cases.expected: 200; a new draft with the same line items and configuration.
cases.oracle: New event group with matching line items and a different ref id.

cases.title: An amendment publish requires non-blank remarks
cases.why: An amendment changes what vendors bid against; the remark is what they are shown.
cases.setup: An amendment draft.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate with blank `amendment_remarks.remarks`, then with real ones.
cases.expected: First refused, second published.
cases.oracle: The amendment is recorded with the remark text. ≈ BE-2.20.

cases.title: An amendment publish with the remarks key absent does not crash
cases.why: The amendment-draft path reads that key directly, so an absent one is a nil-dereference candidate.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate an amendment draft with no `amendment_remarks` at all.
cases.expected: A readable refusal.

cases.title: Ownership changes for the owner, a super admin or a Procol employee, and nobody else
cases.why: It is how an event survives someone leaving the company, and it hands over full control — so the gate matters as much as the feature.
cases.steps: `POST /event_groups/:uuid/change_ownership` as the owner, as a super admin, and as an unrelated buyer.
cases.expected: First two allowed, the third refused.
cases.oracle: Owner reflected after the allowed calls; unchanged after the refusal. ≈ BE-4.10, BE-4.11.

cases.section: Issue a new version of the event — `POST /item_versions`
cases.title: Issue a new version of the event: item_uuid is omitted
cases.why: `item_uuid` is part of the working request for this step; the server must validate it rather than store bad data or fail with a 5xx.
cases.setup: A sandbox event built by the journey up to this step (a second copy, so the journey's own event is untouched).
cases.steps: Send `POST /item_versions` exactly as the journey does. Remove `item_uuid` from the body.
cases.expected: A clean refusal: HTTP 4xx with an error message; nothing is created or changed.
cases.oracle: status in 400–499 (never 2xx, never 5xx); a follow-up read shows no change.

cases.section: Issue a new version of the event — `POST /item_versions`
cases.title: Issue a new version of the event: item_uuid has the wrong type
cases.why: `item_uuid` is part of the working request for this step; the server must validate it rather than store bad data or fail with a 5xx.
cases.setup: A sandbox event built by the journey up to this step (a second copy, so the journey's own event is untouched).
cases.steps: Send `POST /item_versions` exactly as the journey does. Send `item_uuid` as 12345 (it is string in a working request).
cases.expected: A clean refusal: HTTP 4xx with an error message; nothing is created or changed.
cases.oracle: status in 400–499 (never 2xx, never 5xx); a follow-up read shows no change.

cases.section: Issue a new version of the event — `POST /item_versions`
cases.title: Issue a new version of the event answers within 10 seconds
cases.why: A regression that makes a core call several times slower is a defect even when the body is right.
cases.setup: A buyer walking the API journey (RFQ only), at the step "Issue a new version of the event".
cases.steps: 1. As the buyer, do “Issue a new version of the event” in the API journey (`POST /item_versions`). 2. Time the answer.
cases.expected: The app answers within 10 seconds.
cases.oracle: Checked automatically on every API journey run; the report shows what actually came back. Engine check: `max_ms 10000`, learned from 4 real response(s).

cases.title: A withdrawn event can be cloned
cases.why: Deliberately allowed — cloning is how a buyer relaunches an event they had to pull.
cases.steps: `POST create_clone` on a withdrawn event.
cases.expected: Allowed.
cases.oracle: A new draft exists.

cases.title: Cloning a draft is refused
cases.why: Code 1122, "Only active or withdrawn events can be cloned."
cases.steps: `POST create_clone` on a draft.
cases.oracle: No clone created. ≈ BE-8.3.

cases.title: Cloning a PR-created event is refused
cases.why: Code 1123 — the clone would have no requisition behind it.
cases.steps: `POST create_clone` on a PR-created event.
cases.oracle: No clone created. ≈ BE-8.4.

cases.title: A planner cannot clone
cases.why: A policy carve-out that would otherwise pass because cloning needs only create permission.
cases.setup: A planner with create permission.
cases.steps: `POST create_clone`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No clone created. ≈ BE-8.2.

journeys.title: Permissions and isolation
journeys.goal: Each role sees and does only what it should; no vendor sees another's bid.

cases.title: A vendor cannot open an event they were not invited to
cases.why: Direct-URL access is the first thing anyone tries.
cases.setup: An event's URL and an uninvited vendor.
cases.steps: Navigate directly.
cases.expected: Refused, not rendered.
cases.oracle: The event's title and prices are absent from the response.

cases.title: A vendor with no visible stage cannot view the event at all
cases.why: Read permission alone is not enough — the policy also requires at least one visible stage, which is a rule people forget exists.
cases.setup: A vendor on the company's platform but not on any stage's audience.
cases.steps: Attempt to open the event.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Authorization failure rather than an empty event page. Pairs with API-PERM-001.

cases.title: A buyer from another company cannot see the event
cases.why: Cross-tenant isolation, the highest-stakes boundary in the system.
cases.setup: Two companies; an event in company A.
cases.steps: As a buyer in company B, search for and navigate to it.
cases.expected: Not found; direct access refused.
cases.oracle: Zero rows and a refusal.

cases.title: A buyer without trade-create permission cannot create or publish
cases.why: Permissions are team-based here, so a user can look like a buyer and not be one.
cases.setup: A user whose teams grant read but not create on `trade`.
cases.steps: Try to reach the create screen and publish.
cases.expected: Refused or unavailable.
cases.oracle: No event created.

cases.title: Vendor masking removes the Audience tab
cases.why: gate: `isVendorMaskingEnabled`. Masking exists so a buyer's team cannot see who is bidding; leaving the tab in defeats it entirely.
cases.setup: gate: `isVendorMaskingEnabled`.
cases.steps: Open a published event's tabs.
cases.expected: No Audience tab.
cases.oracle: Tab absent from the list.

cases.title: Vendor masking hides vendor identities in the comparison
cases.why: The tab being gone is worthless if the names appear on the grid.
cases.setup: gate: `isVendorMaskingEnabled`. An event with two bids.
cases.steps: Open Master QCS.
cases.expected: Vendors appear as anonymised labels, not company names.
cases.oracle: No real vendor name in the rendered grid **or** in the payload behind it.

cases.title: An evaluator sees the technical response and not the prices
cases.why: The separation of technical and commercial evaluation is the point of a two-stage event.
cases.setup: An RFP + RFQ event with a submitted technical response and a bid.
cases.steps: As the evaluator, open the response.
cases.expected: Questionnaire answers visible; prices not.
cases.oracle: No bid price in the evaluator's view or its payload.

cases.title: A vendor cannot reach the buyer console
cases.why: Two applications, one identity provider — the boundary must hold.
cases.setup: Vendor credentials.
cases.steps: Try to log into the buyer console.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No authenticated buyer session.

cases.title: A buyer cannot place a bid as their own company
cases.why: "Cannot place bid on trade by your own company" (165) — otherwise a buyer could bid against their own event.
cases.setup: A buyer on their own event.
cases.steps: Attempt to bid as the buying company.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: A user without sourcing-events access cannot create a stage
cases.why: `has_access_for_sourcing_events?` is a second, independent gate on stage creation; passing the first and failing this one is a real configuration.
cases.setup: A user with trade-create but without sourcing-events access.
cases.steps: Attempt to create a stage.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No stage created. Pairs with API-PERM-004.

cases.title: Uploading a bid Excel needs view access to the event
cases.why: It is a bulk write path, and bulk write paths with weak authorization are the worst kind.
cases.setup: A user without view access to the event.
cases.steps: Attempt the upload.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bids created.

cases.title: Session expiry mid-journey is handled, not crashed into
cases.why: A long bidding session outlives a token, and the vendor must be told rather than losing a filled sheet to a silent failure.
cases.setup: A filled bid sheet and an expired session.
cases.steps: Submit.
cases.expected: A re-authentication prompt or a clear message; the entered values are not lost without warning.
cases.oracle: A readable message rather than a blank screen or a swallowed error.

cases.title: A planner cannot clone an event
cases.why: A specific policy carve-out that would otherwise pass silently because cloning needs only create permission.
cases.setup: A planner with create permission.
cases.steps: Try to clone an active event.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No clone created.

cases.title: Feedback on a bid is restricted to the order's team or a super admin
cases.why: A narrow gate on an otherwise open bid policy, so it is easy to lose in a refactor.
cases.setup: A buyer not on the order's team and not a super admin.
cases.steps: Attempt to add feedback on a bid.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No feedback recorded. Pairs with API-PERM-011.

cases.title: `GET /api/event_groups` requires trade read permission
cases.why: The listing is the module's front door.
cases.steps: List as a user with trade read, then as one without.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: Both outcomes.

cases.title: `GET /api/event_groups/:id` requires read *and* a visible stage
cases.why: Two conditions, and the second is the one people forget — a user with read access and no visible stage is refused.
cases.steps: Read as the owner, then as a user with trade read but no stage visibility.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: No event payload in the refusal. ≈ BE-8.1.

cases.title: `POST /api/event_groups` requires trade create permission
cases.why: The privileged write in the module.
cases.steps: Create with and without the permission.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One event group created in total. ≈ BE-1.7.

cases.title: Event-group update accepts either policy branch and refuses outside both
cases.why: The policy is a two-branch OR (Procol CSM, or allowed-company plus trade create). Testing one branch proves half a rule.
cases.steps: `PATCH` as a CSM Procol employee, as an in-company buyer with create, and as a user in neither category.
cases.expected: First two allowed, third refused.
cases.oracle: All three outcomes.

cases.title: Proposal endpoints all sit behind `add_response?`
cases.why: Show, submit, the approval lookup and discard share one policy method — so one hole opens four endpoints.
cases.steps: Call each of the four as a caller outside the allowed companies.
cases.expected: All four refused.
cases.oracle: Four refusals; no proposal state changes.

cases.title: A vendor cannot call any buyer write endpoint
cases.why: A sweep rather than a single case — it is the cheapest way to catch a newly added endpoint with no policy.
cases.steps: As a vendor session, call event-group create/update, stage create, proposal create and close_bid.
cases.expected: All refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created by any of them; add new write endpoints to this sweep as they appear.

cases.title: Stage creation requires create permission *and* sourcing-events access
cases.why: Two independent gates; a user can pass the first and fail the second, which is a real configuration.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/template_input` as a user with both, then with only create.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One stage created in total. ≈ BE-8.7.

cases.title: Stage update allows a Procol employee unconditionally
cases.why: A support back door, and back doors need their own cases so nobody removes them accidentally — or widens them.
cases.steps: `PATCH /trade/:id` as a Procol employee outside the company.
cases.expected: Allowed.
cases.oracle: The update applies; then confirm a non-employee outside the company is refused.

cases.title: Clone requires allowed company, create permission, non-planner, non-draft, non-PR
cases.why: Five conditions on one endpoint; each is its own way in.
cases.steps: Vary one condition at a time from a known-good clone.
cases.expected: The good case succeeds; each variation is refused.
cases.oracle: Exactly one clone created across the whole set.

cases.title: Vendor self-participation requires show access and open tenders
cases.why: `participate?` is `show? && open_tenders?` — again two conditions.
cases.steps: Participate as an invited vendor on an open-tender event, then as an uninvited vendor, then on a non-open-tender event.
cases.expected: First allowed, other two refused.
cases.oracle: One audience row created in total.

cases.title: `update_egli` needs stage-update rights *and* the evaluation window
cases.why: The policy allows it while the inline time check still refuses — two layers, and a test that only has permission passes wrongly.
cases.steps: Call it with rights inside the window, with rights outside it, and without rights inside it.
cases.expected: Only the first succeeds.
cases.oracle: Evaluators change exactly once. ≈ BE-3.5.

cases.title: Surrogate approval-flow reads need approval-flow read permission
cases.why: The other gated bid-policy method, and an empty list would read as "no approval needed".
cases.steps: Call it with and without the permission.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused — not an empty success.
cases.oracle: Both outcomes. ≈ BE-5.5.

cases.title: Live-auction audience edits need view access
cases.why: A narrow gate on a write that changes who can bid.
cases.steps: Add an audience with and without view access.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One audience row. ≈ BE-4.9.

cases.title: Every 403/422 refusal leaks nothing about the resource
cases.why: A refusal that echoes the event's title or the vendor's name is an information leak dressed as an authorization success.
cases.steps: Collect the bodies of ten refusals from this section.
cases.expected: Each carries a code and a generic message only.
cases.oracle: No titles, vendor names or prices in any refusal body.

cases.title: Vendor-onboarding-v2 stage updates need the onboarding permission
cases.why: A mode-specific extra gate that a generic stage-update test would miss entirely.
cases.setup: A vendor-onboarding-v2 stage and a user without that permission.
cases.steps: `PATCH /trade/:id`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No update applied. ≈ BE-8.6.

cases.title: Bid feedback needs the order's team or super admin plus the config
cases.why: One of the two genuinely gated bid-policy methods.
cases.steps: Add feedback as a team member, then as an outsider.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One feedback record. ≈ BE-5.4.

cases.title: Contract-form creation needs `add_response?` *and* the tenant config
cases.why: A config gate stacked on a policy gate.
cases.steps: Call it with the policy satisfied and the config off.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No contract form. ≈ BE-6.4.

cases.title: Restricted admin operations are limited to an explicit allow-list
cases.why: Some maintenance endpoints are restricted to named Procol employees; an allow-list that stops being enforced is a privileged-access failure.
cases.steps: Call the restricted operation as a non-listed Procol employee.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing regenerated or changed. ≈ BE-8.8.

journeys.title: Validation and robustness
journeys.goal: The product refuses bad input with the right message, persists correctly, and stays within its performance budget.

cases.title: The console recovers from a backend 5xx without losing the form
cases.why: During the activation regression every publish failed; how the screen behaved then decided whether buyers lost their work as well as their event.
cases.setup: A create screen with a full configuration; force a 5xx on publish.
cases.steps: Publish. Read the screen.
cases.expected: An error is surfaced and every entered value is still there.
cases.oracle: The form retains its values; a message is visible.

cases.title: Every required field on the create screen is enforced
cases.why: It is the requirement stated most broadly in the PRD, so it needs a systematic case rather than one per field.
cases.setup: A create screen.
cases.steps: Attempt publish with each required field blank in turn — title, template, line items, schedule, participants.
cases.expected: Each is refused with a message naming the field. No partial event.
cases.oracle: For each: publish blocked, message present, and zero events created.

cases.title: HTML in a title is escaped, not rendered
cases.why: Stored XSS in an event title would reach every invited vendor.
cases.steps: Title ``. Publish. View the list, the detail page and the vendor's portal.
cases.expected: The text renders literally; no script executes anywhere.
cases.oracle: No dialog/console error; the DOM contains escaped text, not an element.

cases.title: A script payload in a line-item or clause field is escaped
cases.why: Titles are the obvious field; clauses and item descriptions reach vendors too.
cases.steps: Put the same payload in a T&C clause and an item description. Publish. View as the vendor.
cases.expected: Escaped everywhere.
cases.oracle: No execution in either view.

cases.title: A malformed request never produces a partial event
cases.why: PRD §5's "no partial record" clause. A half-written event is worse than a refused one because nobody knows it exists.
cases.setup: A crafted create request with a malformed `line_items` (a string, not an array).
cases.steps: Send it.
cases.expected: A 4xx with a readable message; nothing written.
cases.oracle: No event group and no line items created. Pairs with API-VAL-003.

cases.title: A failed request does not leave the screen in a dead state
cases.why: After the activation regression, the button did nothing and the buyer had no idea why — the absence of feedback was as damaging as the failure.
cases.setup: Any refused publish.
cases.steps: After the refusal, try to correct the problem and publish again.
cases.expected: The screen is still usable; the second attempt works.
cases.oracle: No reload needed to recover; the retry succeeds.

cases.title: Publishing a 500-item event completes within a stated budget
cases.why: A publish that times out client-side while succeeding server-side is the worst outcome: the buyer retries and creates a second event.
cases.setup: A 500-item BOQ event.
cases.steps: Publish and time it.
cases.expected: Completes; the client waits long enough. If it times out, the event must not be duplicated by a retry.
cases.oracle: One event afterwards, whatever the timing; record the duration.

cases.title: A slow network does not double-submit a bid
cases.why: Vendors bid on bad connections at the last minute; a duplicate bid is a real integrity problem.
cases.setup: Throttled network, a live event.
cases.steps: Submit a bid and click again while it is in flight.
cases.expected: One bid.
cases.oracle: Bid count = 1 on the buyer's side.

cases.title: A dropped connection mid-publish leaves a recoverable state
cases.why: PRD §7.3 — a half-finished action must corrupt nothing.
cases.setup: A valid event.
cases.steps: Kill the network during the publish request. Restore it. Reload.
cases.expected: Either published or still a draft; never a broken half-state, and never two events.
cases.oracle: Exactly one event with that title, in a coherent status.

cases.title: The bid countdown agrees with the server's clock
cases.why: A vendor bidding against a fast client clock loses the event through no fault of their own.
cases.setup: A live event near its end.
cases.steps: Compare the rendered countdown with the server's end time.
cases.expected: Within a couple of seconds.
cases.oracle: Difference under a small threshold; a client-clock skew must not shift it.

cases.title: Two buyers editing one draft do not silently overwrite each other
cases.why: The version guard exists for this, and the failure mode is losing a colleague's work without either of them knowing.
cases.setup: One draft, two buyers.
cases.steps: Both edit; both save.
cases.expected: The second save is either merged or refused as stale, with a message.
cases.oracle: No silent loss: after both saves, the surviving state is explainable and the loser was told. Pairs with UI-PUB-011.

cases.title: A whitespace-only title is treated as blank
cases.why: It is the standard way past a presence check.
cases.steps: Title `" "`. Publish.
cases.expected: Refused as missing.
cases.oracle: Publish blocked.

cases.title: SQL-ish input is handled as text
cases.why: `'; DROP TABLE` in a search box is the cheapest smoke test for a whole class of failure.
cases.steps: Search the events list and the participant list for `'; DROP TABLE event_groups; --`.
cases.expected: Zero or literal matches; no error.
cases.oracle: A normal empty-result state; no 500.

cases.title: A very long string in every text field is bounded politely
cases.why: PRD §6. Unbounded fields become database errors, which become 500s.
cases.steps: Enter 10,000 characters into the title, description and a clause.
cases.expected: Either accepted whole or refused with a stated limit. No 500, no silent truncation.
cases.oracle: Per field: a message, or a value that round-trips exactly.

cases.title: More decimal places than the template allows are rounded visibly
cases.why: Silent rounding of a price changes the bid.
cases.steps: Enter `100.999` where 2 decimals are configured.
cases.expected: Rounded to `101.00` **and** shown that way before submission.
cases.oracle: Displayed and stored values agree.

cases.title: Duplicate product names in master data do not confuse the picker
cases.why: PRD §6 lists duplicate product names; the picker must disambiguate or the buyer adds the wrong item.
cases.setup: Two products with the same name and different codes.
cases.steps: Search for the name in the line-items picker.
cases.expected: Both are offered, distinguishable (code, category or variant).
cases.oracle: Two options with distinguishing text; the chosen one is the one that lands.

cases.title: A duplicate user email is refused when adding a user
cases.why: PRD §6, and duplicated identities break team-based permissions.
cases.setup: An existing user's email.
cases.steps: Create a user with the same email.
cases.expected: Refused with a readable message.
cases.oracle: No second user created.

cases.title: A 10-digit phone number is accepted and stored with a country prefix
cases.why: The PRD states this as an acceptance criterion *and* flags it for verification: the specified rule is "any 10-digit number, prefixed `+91` by default". If the product is stricter or looser, the difference is the finding.
cases.setup: The user-create form.
cases.steps: Enter `9876543210` and save. Then try `1234567890`, `0000000000`, a 9-digit and an 11-digit number.
cases.expected: All 10-digit values accepted and stored as `+91…`; 9- and 11-digit refused.
cases.oracle: Record the exact behaviour per input and compare against the specified rule — this case is expected to produce a finding either way.

cases.title: An invalid email format is refused
cases.why: PRD §5 names email format explicitly, and it is the field most often loosely validated.
cases.steps: Try `a@`, `a@b`, `a b@c.com`, `a@@b.com`.
cases.expected: All refused with a format message.
cases.oracle: No record created for any of them.

cases.title: Every validation message is readable and names the problem
cases.why: PRD §5's "politely" clause is a real requirement. `Error 712` on screen is a defect even when the refusal is correct.
cases.setup: Any five refusal paths from this catalog.
cases.steps: Trigger each and read the message.
cases.expected: Each is a sentence naming the problem, not a bare code.
cases.oracle: No message consists only of a number; each contains a field or an action.

cases.title: The events list stays under the 3-second target as volume grows
cases.why: PRD §7.1, measured rather than assumed.
cases.setup: Tenants with ~10, ~100 and ~1000 events.
cases.steps: Time a cold load of the list on each.
cases.expected: Under ~3s throughout.
cases.oracle: Record the three numbers and trend them; flag regressions rather than asserting a hard threshold on shared infrastructure.

cases.title: The create screen stays responsive with 65 line items
cases.why: The sheet is the heaviest component in the product and the cap is the realistic worst case for a non-BOQ event.
cases.setup: A non-BOQ event at the cap.
cases.steps: Scroll and edit cells at the top and bottom of the sheet.
cases.expected: Edits register without visible lag; no dropped keystrokes.
cases.oracle: Every value entered is present after the pass.

cases.title: A 500-row BOQ sheet renders and can be scrolled
cases.why: PRD §6's large-event case, at the UI layer.
cases.setup: A 500-item BOQ event.
cases.steps: Open the sheet; scroll to the last row.
cases.expected: It renders (virtualised is fine) and the last row is reachable.
cases.oracle: Row 500 is present and correct.

cases.title: Accessibility basics on the create and bid screens
cases.why: They are the two screens people spend hours in, and the automation depends on roles and labels to find anything at all — so it is also a testability matter.
cases.setup: The create screen and the vendor bid sheet.
cases.steps: Tab through each; check that every control has an accessible name.
cases.expected: Focus order follows the visual order; no unlabelled interactive control.
cases.oracle: An accessibility scan with zero critical violations on named controls.

cases.title: Emoji survive in titles, descriptions and clauses
cases.why: Four-byte characters are where encoding assumptions break.
cases.steps: Use emoji in each. Publish. Read back on the buyer's and vendor's views.
cases.expected: Identical rendering everywhere.
cases.oracle: Byte equality on read-back.

cases.title: Leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed consistently
cases.why: `"RFQ "` and `"RFQ"` as two different titles makes search unreliable for everyone.
cases.steps: Publish with `" Event A "`. Search for `"Event A"`.
cases.expected: Found; the stored title is trimmed.
cases.oracle: Search hit and an exact stored value.

cases.title: A number field rejects `e`-notation and thousands separators
cases.why: `1e5` and `1,00,000` both parse to something unexpected somewhere in the stack.
cases.steps: Enter `1e5` and `1,00,000` into a price cell.
cases.expected: Refused or normalised visibly. Not stored as an unrelated number.
cases.oracle: The stored value equals what is displayed.

cases.title: Right-to-left and CJK text render without breaking layout
cases.why: Real tenants have them, and a broken grid is unusable rather than merely ugly.
cases.steps: Enter Arabic and Chinese text in a title and a line-item description.
cases.expected: Rendered correctly; the sheet's columns stay aligned.
cases.oracle: No horizontal overflow of the grid container; text matches.

cases.title: A created event group exists as a row
cases.why: It is the PRD requirement in its most literal form.
cases.steps: Create a draft. Query `event_groups` by uuid.
cases.expected: One row with status draft and the caller's company and user.
cases.oracle: Row present with those columns. `src/db/verify.ts`.

cases.title: The event group belongs to the acting workspace
cases.why: For a multi-company user, the wrong `company_id` writes an event into another tenant.
cases.steps: Create as a multi-company user in company A. Read the row.
cases.expected: `company_id` is A.
cases.oracle: Column equals A's id.

cases.title: A published stage has a bidding-time schedule row with a non-null end time
cases.why: It is the row whose absence is the top suspect for the activation 500, and `end_time` is `NOT NULL` at the database level.
cases.steps: Publish. Query `trade_schedules` for the stage.
cases.expected: A bidding-time row with both times set.
cases.oracle: Row present; `end_time` not null. This is the definitive form of API-STG-014.

cases.title: A submitted bid and its products are persisted with the right prices
cases.why: The bid is the commercial artefact; if the row disagrees with the API response, the award is built on the wrong number.
cases.steps: Submit a bid. Query the bid and its products.
cases.expected: One active bid with one product row per line item, prices as submitted.
cases.oracle: Row-level equality with the submitted payload.

cases.title: Nothing is written when a create or activation is refused
cases.why: PRD §5's "no partial record" clause, verified where it actually matters. During the activation regression this was the one reassuring fact: nothing was written.
cases.steps: For five refusal paths in this file, count the relevant rows before and after.
cases.expected: Identical counts.
cases.oracle: Row counts for `event_groups`, `event_group_line_items`, `trade_requests`, `trade_schedules`, `audiences` and `bids` unchanged.

cases.title: Errors follow one shape across the module
cases.why: The whole regression guard rests on this convention: failures are `{code, message}` with a 422, so an untyped 500 is definitionally an exception.
cases.steps: Collect twenty refusals from across this file.
cases.expected: Every one carries a numeric code and a human message.
cases.oracle: No refusal without a code; report any that lack one.

cases.title: Idempotency holds for every write in this file
cases.why: A sweep rather than a single case; retries are the norm and the cost of a duplicate differs wildly by endpoint.
cases.steps: Repeat each write endpoint's happy-path call once.
cases.expected: No duplicates of events, stages, audiences, bids or proposals.
cases.oracle: Row counts unchanged after the repeat; where a duplicate is created deliberately, document why.

cases.title: Every required parameter is enforced on every write endpoint
cases.why: It is the broadest requirement in the PRD; a systematic sweep beats one case per field.
cases.steps: For event-group create/update, stage create, bid create and proposal create: omit each required parameter in turn.
cases.expected: 422 with code 2 (or the endpoint's specific code) each time.
cases.oracle: Nothing created in any variation.

cases.title: Unknown parameters are ignored, not persisted
cases.why: An endpoint that stores whatever it is sent is a mass-assignment risk.
cases.steps: Send `{"is_admin": true, "company_id": <another company>}` alongside a valid create.
cases.expected: Created, with those values ignored.
cases.oracle: The created row's company is the caller's own.

cases.title: A malformed body type is refused, not coerced
cases.why: PRD §5's "no partial record" clause.
cases.steps: Send `line_items` as a string, `config` as an array, `quantity` as an object where a number belongs.
cases.expected: 4xx with a readable message each time.
cases.oracle: No 500; nothing created. ≈ BE-1.12.

cases.title: A fabricated uuid is refused with a not-found code
cases.why: Every id-taking endpoint should answer 533/95/32/250 as appropriate rather than raising.
cases.steps: Call event-group show/update, trade show, bid show and proposal show with fabricated ids.
cases.expected: The appropriate not-found code each time.
cases.oracle: No 500 in any case.

cases.title: Another company's id is refused, not treated as not-found
cases.why: The distinction matters: "not found" for a resource that exists elsewhere is acceptable, but succeeding is a cross-tenant breach.
cases.steps: Read and update company B's event group from a company A session.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No payload and no write.

cases.title: A script payload in a text field is stored inert
cases.why: Event titles reach every invited vendor's screen — stored XSS here has the widest blast radius in the product.
cases.steps: Create an event whose title is ``. Read it as the buyer and as a vendor.
cases.expected: Stored and returned as text.
cases.oracle: The response is escaped or plainly text; the UI counterpart is UI-VAL-003.

cases.title: A concurrent double activation produces one published event
cases.why: The `lock_transaction` on this endpoint exists for it — and a double-render on a held lock is the top-ranked cause of the standing 500.
cases.steps: Fire two activations for the same event group simultaneously.
cases.expected: One activation; the other refused with a lock/conflict code.
cases.oracle: One set of stages and audiences. If the loser returns an untyped 500, that confirms the double-render candidate — record the exception class.

cases.title: The reference id is assigned and unique
cases.why: `add_ref_id` uses `update_columns`, bypassing validations — so uniqueness is not enforced by the model.
cases.steps: Create three events. Read their ref ids.
cases.expected: Three non-null, distinct ids.
cases.oracle: Distinctness across the three.

cases.title: Line-item rows carry their serial numbers and statuses
cases.why: Serials order the sheet and the award; statuses drive every read filter.
cases.steps: Create two line items. Read `event_group_line_items`.
cases.expected: Two active rows with serials 1 and 2.
cases.oracle: Rows, serials and statuses.

cases.title: Audience rows are unique per company, item and visibility while active
cases.why: The model's own invariant, and duplicate active rows double-count a vendor everywhere downstream.
cases.steps: Publish, then re-publish. Query `audiences`.
cases.expected: One active row per company per stage.
cases.oracle: No duplicate `(audience_id, item_id, item_type, visible)` among active rows.

cases.title: A withdrawn event's status and remark are persisted
cases.why: The remark is the audit trail and it lives in the row, not in the response.
cases.steps: Withdraw. Query the event group.
cases.expected: Status withdrawn with the remark stored.
cases.oracle: Status column and remark content.

cases.title: A voided stage is marked void and stays out of every read
cases.why: `void` means "remove from everywhere" — a void stage that still appears in a read is a ghost that can accept bids.
cases.steps: Publish two of three stages. Query the third.
cases.expected: Status void; absent from every API read.
cases.oracle: Row status and API absence together.

cases.title: Activating a 500-line-item event completes
cases.why: PRD §6's large-event case at the heaviest write in the module.
cases.setup: A BOQ event with 500 line items.
cases.steps: Activate and time it.
cases.expected: Completes without a timeout.
cases.oracle: 200 within the client's timeout; record the duration.

cases.title: Concurrent bids from many vendors are all recorded
cases.why: An auction's last minute *is* a concurrency test, and a lost bid is a lost vendor.
cases.steps: Submit bids from 20 vendors simultaneously on one stage.
cases.expected: All 20 recorded, correctly ranked.
cases.oracle: 20 bid rows; ranks consistent with the prices.

cases.title: Timestamps and timezones are consistent across reads
cases.why: Buyer and vendor must agree on when bidding ends; a mixed representation is a fairness bug.
cases.steps: Read one event's window through the event-group, trade and vendor-facing endpoints.
cases.expected: The same instant everywhere, in one representation.
cases.oracle: Normalise all three to UTC and compare.

cases.title: Invalid JSON is refused cleanly
cases.why: The framework's default answer to broken JSON is easy to leave as a 500.
cases.steps: `POST` a truncated JSON body.
cases.expected: A 4xx.
cases.oracle: Not a 500.

cases.title: An id of the wrong type is refused
cases.why: `"abc"` or `null` where an integer or uuid belongs is a classic 500.
cases.steps: Call the same endpoints with `"abc"`, `null` and `-1`.
cases.expected: 4xx each time.

cases.title: Very long strings are bounded politely
cases.why: PRD §6. An unbounded string field becomes a database error, which becomes a 500.
cases.steps: Send a 100,000-character title, description and clause.
cases.expected: Either accepted or refused with a stated limit. No 500, no silent truncation.
cases.oracle: Compare the stored value to what was sent.

cases.title: Emoji and multi-byte text round-trip byte for byte
cases.why: Four-byte characters are where encoding and column charset assumptions break.
cases.steps: Create an event with emoji and CJK text in the title and a line-item description. Read it back.
cases.expected: Byte-identical.
cases.oracle: Exact equality on read-back, and again in the database. ≈ PRD §6.

cases.title: Numeric edge values are handled or refused explicitly
cases.why: `0`, huge values, high precision and `e`-notation each fail differently.
cases.steps: Send `0`, `999999999999.99`, `1e10`, `0.000001` as prices and quantities.
cases.expected: Each either accepted with the exact value preserved or refused with a message.
cases.oracle: The stored value equals the sent value wherever accepted.

cases.title: Epoch times outside a sane range are refused
cases.why: Schedules take epoch seconds; `0` and year-3000 values would create events nobody can bid on and reports nobody can read.
cases.steps: Send `bid_start_time: 0`, a negative value, and a value 100 years out.
cases.expected: Refused, or accepted with a documented clamp.
cases.oracle: No schedule row with an absurd time.

cases.title: SQL-ish input is treated as data
cases.why: The cheapest probe for a whole class of failure, and search endpoints are the usual place it is missed.
cases.steps: Send `'; DROP TABLE event_groups; --` to product search, vendor search and the events filter.
cases.expected: Empty or literal results; no error.
cases.oracle: Normal responses; the table still exists (a subsequent read succeeds).

cases.title: Duplicate creation requests do not produce duplicate events
cases.why: A retried create is the most common client behaviour on a slow network.
cases.steps: Send the identical create twice.
cases.expected: Either one event, or two with distinct ids and a documented behaviour.
cases.oracle: Record which; if two events result, flag it as a finding for the UI's double-submit case (UI-PUB-007).

cases.title: A duplicate user email is refused on user create
cases.why: PRD §6, and duplicated identities break team-based permissions.
cases.steps: `POST /users/create_user` twice with the same email.
cases.expected: The second refused with a readable message.
cases.oracle: One user. `flows/masterData.ts`.

cases.title: The phone rule is verified against the PRD's stated criterion
cases.why: The PRD states "any 10-digit number, stored with a `+91` prefix by default" **and explicitly asks QA to verify the claim**. If the product is stricter or looser, the difference is the deliverable.
cases.steps: `POST /users/create_user` with `9876543210`, `1234567890`, `0000000000`, a 9-digit and an 11-digit number.
cases.expected: All 10-digit values accepted and stored as `+91…`; 9 and 11 digits refused.
cases.oracle: Record the stored value for each input and diff against the specified rule. This case is expected to produce a finding either way.

cases.title: The events listing responds inside the performance budget
cases.why: PRD §7.1, measured at the API layer where the number is clean.
cases.steps: `GET /api/event_groups` on tenants with ~10, ~100 and ~1000 events.
cases.expected: Under ~3 seconds throughout.
cases.oracle: Record the three timings and trend them.

cases.title: Reading an event with 500 line items and 100 bids stays usable
cases.why: The show action builds the whole project payload — widgets, layers, proposals, approvals — and it is where a large event first becomes unusable.
cases.steps: `GET /api/event_groups/:id` on such an event.
cases.expected: A complete response in reasonable time.
cases.oracle: Response completeness and duration recorded.

cases.title: Rate limiting, if present, answers with a code rather than a 500
cases.why: A suite that trips a rate limit should be able to tell that apart from a real failure.
cases.steps: Issue a burst of reads.
cases.expected: Either all succeed or a rate-limit response identifies itself.
cases.oracle: No untyped 500 in the burst.

cases.title: Epoch times as strings are handled consistently
cases.why: Clients send `"1757404800"` as often as the integer; silently parsing one and not the other creates a phantom scheduling bug.
cases.steps: Send both forms.
cases.expected: Both accepted identically, or the string refused with a message.
cases.oracle: The resulting schedules are identical, or the refusal is explicit.

journeys.title: Setting up the tenant: master data, admin and platform settings
journeys.goal: Load the master data (users, materials, services, UOM, tax), set up SSO, roles and data visibility, and configure approval matrices, cost centres and reporting.

cases.title: Template Management & Versioning: happy path for the Tenant Admin
cases.why: Safe configuration lifecycle. Business use: Admins manage templates with versioning/revert and promote them from UAT to PROD.
cases.setup: Persona: Tenant Admin. Plan: tenant on Enterprise (lowest plan with access; Plan Required: Enterprise). Status: GA.
cases.steps: 1. Sign in as a Tenant Admin on the tenant described in Setup and open Admin & Configuration. 2. Use Template Management & Versioning to get what the story asks for: template versioning and UAT-to-PROD promotion. 3. Follow the business scenario the workbook gives: "Admins manage templates with versioning/revert and promote them from UAT to PROD". 4. Check the result against the story's promised outcome.
cases.expected: The Tenant Admin achieves the story's outcome: evolve configurations safely. The business use case is served: admins manage templates with versioning/revert and promote them from UAT to PROD.
cases.oracle: Observable proof that Template Management & Versioning did its job for the Tenant Admin — the outcome in Expected is visible in Procol after the last step, with no error, on the plan in Setup. Any gap is a defect against FEAT-ADM-002.

cases.title: Platform-Wide Activity & Audit Log: happy path for the Auditor
cases.why: Compliance and traceability. Business use: Auditors trace any action via the platform-wide activity/audit log, including project-level and live-event changes.
cases.setup: Persona: Auditor. Plan: any tenant (Plan Required: All Plans). Status: GA.
cases.steps: 1. Sign in as an Auditor on the tenant described in Setup and open Admin & Configuration. 2. Use Platform-Wide Activity & Audit Log to get what the story asks for: a complete platform-wide activity log. 3. Follow the business scenario the workbook gives: "Auditors trace any action via the platform-wide activity/audit log, including project-level and live-event changes". 4. Check the result against the story's promised outcome.
cases.expected: The Auditor achieves the story's outcome: trace any action. The business use case is served: auditors trace any action via the platform-wide activity/audit log, including project-level and live-event changes.

cases.section: How to Create RFQ and Auction Templates
cases.title: Create and publish an RFQ/Auction template
cases.why: Templates predefine formats, terms, awarding rules and data fields; an RFQ or Auction event is launched from a published template.
cases.setup: Buyer user with access to **Manage › Templates**.
cases.steps: 1. From the homepage, go to the **Manage** tab in the left navigation. 2. Hover over **Manage** and click **Templates**. 3. Click **Create Template**, hover over it and select **RFQ/Auction**. 4. On the Template Creation page, enter the **Template Title** and verify the category is **RFQ/Auction**. 5. Click **Ranking Criteria** and set the awarding criteria and **Template Type**. 6. Click **Add**, choose a column type and configure the column. 7. Click the blue **"Publish"** button.
cases.expected: The template is published and can be used for future RFQs and Auctions.
cases.oracle: Published-template confirmation is shown; the template is available when creating a future RFQ / Auction.

cases.section: How to Create RFQ and Auction Templates
cases.title: Quote Sheet per line item vs single Global Sheet
cases.why: Fields placed on the wrong sheet are either repeated per line item or asked once per event.
cases.setup: A published RFQ/Auction template with fields on both the Quote Sheet and the Global Sheet; an event created from it with two or more line items.
cases.steps: 1. In the template, add a field to the Quote Sheet and a field to the Global Sheet. 2. Create an event from the template with multiple line items and view the sheets.
cases.expected: The Quote Sheet (line-item-specific fields) is duplicated for each line item; there is only one Global Sheet (fields applicable across the entire event).
cases.oracle: Quote Sheet field appears once per line item; Global Sheet field appears once for the event.

cases.section: How to Create RFQ and Auction Templates
cases.title: Precision for number-based fields is limited to 0–4 decimals

cases.steps: 1. Open the column's precision setting. 2. Set precision to 0, then 4. 3. Try to set a precision above 4.
cases.expected: Precision 0 through 4 is accepted; nothing beyond 4 decimal positions can be set.
cases.oracle: Precision control offers / accepts only 0–4.

cases.section: How to Create RFQ and Auction Templates
cases.title: Mandatory toggle makes the field required
cases.why: Mandatory fields must be filled in; missing required data breaks evaluation.

cases.steps: 1. Turn on the **Mandatory** toggle for a column and publish. 2. In an event from this template, try to proceed without filling that field.
cases.expected: The field must be filled in.
cases.oracle: The field is flagged as required and the response is not accepted while it is empty.

cases.section: How to Create RFQ and Auction Templates

cases.expected: The field is not visible to vendors.
cases.oracle: The field is absent in the vendor's view while present in the buyer's view.

cases.section: How to Create RFQ and Auction Templates
cases.title: Creator/Participant Field decides who fills the field
cases.why: Assigning a field to the wrong side means it is filled by the wrong party.
cases.setup: RFQ/Auction template; an event from it with an invited vendor.
cases.steps: 1. Set one column as a Creator field and another as a Participant field; publish. 2. Create an event from the template and view it as buyer and as vendor.
cases.expected: The Creator field is filled by the event creator; the Participant field is filled by the vendor.
cases.oracle: Each field is fillable only by the party it is assigned to.

cases.oracle: Evidence of exactly this handling is visible (state, alert, log or retry record as named) and nothing is silently dropped.

cases.section: Roadmap features — not in the product yet (acceptance specifications)

cases.why: The workbook says "SLA duration configurable per module/approval level". A setting a tenant can change is a gate: the feature must follow whatever the tenant chose, for every allowed choice.

cases.steps: 1. As a Tenant Admin, find the tenant setting the note refers to ("SLA duration configurable per module/approval level") and record its current value. 2. As the Tenant Admin: use Approval Escalation on SLA Breach to get approvals pending beyond an SLA to escalate automatically. 3. Change the setting to a different allowed value, then repeat step 2.
cases.expected: In both runs Approval Escalation on SLA Breach follows the tenant's configured value, as the workbook states: "SLA duration configurable per module/approval level". Changing the setting changes the behaviour accordingly.
cases.oracle: The behaviour observed in step 2 and step 3 differs exactly as the two configured values dictate; identical behaviour under different settings means the setting is ignored.

journeys.title: Onboarding and managing a vendor
journeys.goal: Invite or import a vendor, let them self-register and submit onboarding with verified documents, route it through onboarding approval, activate it and sync it to SAP — then amend, extend or block it over its life.

cases.section: How do I Start Onboarding a Vendor?
cases.title: Un-onboarded vendors cannot participate in sourcing events
cases.why: The article states that when onboarding is enabled, vendors cannot participate in RFQs, RFPs or Auctions until onboarded — a compliance gate.
cases.setup: Onboarding enabled; a prospect (invited, not onboarded) and a live RFQ.
cases.steps: 1. Try to have the prospect take part in the RFQ (repeat for an RFP and an Auction). 2. Check the prospect's vendor portal.
cases.expected: Until onboarded, the vendor cannot participate in the sourcing events.
cases.oracle: The prospect cannot take part in the events; after onboarding the same vendor can.

cases.title: Vendor completes and submits the onboarding form
cases.why: Onboarding collects company, GST/PAN, banking and compliance details the buyer needs before events or POs.
cases.setup: Vendor logged into the vendor portal; the buyer has started a Vendor Onboarding Event for them.
cases.steps: 1. Click the Vendor Onboarding Event card. 2. On the Event Overview screen, click the blue **"I will participate"** button. 3. Go to the tab next to "Event Overview" (if not taken there automatically). 4. Fill the form, including all Mandatory fields across the sections. 5. Scroll to the bottom and click "Submit".
cases.expected: A confirmation appears at the top of the screen; the response is submitted and awaits evaluation by the buyer.
cases.oracle: Top-of-screen confirmation; submitted state "You have successfully submitted your vendor onboarding form response!".

cases.title: Vendor cannot access events or receive POs until onboarding is approved
cases.why: The article states that until onboarding is completed and approved by the buyer, the vendor cannot access events or receive POs.
cases.setup: Vendor who has submitted onboarding but is not yet approved; a live event and a PO flow on the buyer side.
cases.steps: 1. As the buyer, try to include the vendor in an event and raise a PO to them. 2. As the vendor, check the portal for the event / PO. 3. Approve the onboarding and repeat.
cases.expected: Before approval the vendor cannot access events or receive POs; after approval they can.
cases.oracle: Event / PO not available to the vendor before approval; available after.

cases.title: Approve the onboarding response and send for approval
cases.why: Approval routes the prospect through the approval workflow that makes them a Joined vendor.
cases.setup: Buyer on a prospect's Onboarding Details in the evaluation stage; an approval workflow configured.
cases.steps: 1. Review the response and click **Approve**. 2. In the send for Approval tab, fill the Buyer Added Attributes form if shown, then click "**Next**". 3. On the Vendor/Prospect summary, add a Category and Location and press "**Next**". 4. Add remarks, observe the approval workflow to be triggered, and click **Continue**.
cases.expected: The prospect is sent for approval.
cases.oracle: Confirmation "The prospect has been sent for Approval".

cases.title: Approver approves and the vendor becomes Joined
cases.why: Final approval makes the vendor onboarded and eligible for any event.
cases.setup: A prospect sent for approval (PRD-KBVON-037); approver user in the workflow.
cases.steps: 1. Sign in as the approver. 2. **Approve** the prospect from the approver's account. 3. As the buyer, check the vendor's status.
cases.expected: The vendor is onboarded, placed into **"Joined"** status, and eligible to be invited to any event.
cases.oracle: Vendor status shows Joined; vendor can be invited to an event.

cases.title: Evaluator rejects the vendor's onboarding response
cases.why: Reject is the other evaluation outcome the article offers; a rejected vendor must not become Joined.
cases.setup: Buyer on a prospect's Onboarding Details in the evaluation stage.
cases.steps: 1. Review the response and click **Reject**. 2. Check the vendor's status.
cases.expected: The vendor is rejected (the article does not describe the resulting status).
cases.oracle: Vendor is not in Joined status; tester records the status shown.

cases.title: Approver rejects the prospect sent for approval
cases.why: The approver can Approve or Reject; a rejection must stop the vendor from being onboarded.
cases.setup: A prospect sent for approval; approver user in the workflow.
cases.steps: 1. Sign in as the approver. 2. **Reject** the prospect from the approver's account. 3. As the buyer, check the vendor's status.
cases.expected: The prospect is not onboarded (the article does not describe the resulting status).
cases.oracle: Vendor is not in Joined status; tester records the status shown.

cases.title: Score a vendor with an Evaluation Matrix
cases.why: The PQ Score is the numerical rating buyers use for risk assessment before onboarding or awarding business.
cases.setup: Buyer user; a vendor whose onboarding response is on the Onboarding Details tab; an evaluation matrix exists.
cases.steps: 1. Go to the **Vendors** tab, open the vendor profile and click **Onboarding Details**. 2. Click **Start Evaluation** (top-right). 3. Scroll to the **Evaluation Matrix Type** dropdown and choose the relevant matrix. 4. For each question in the sections that appear, enter a response and assign a score.
cases.expected: Selecting a matrix shows multiple sections and questions; responses and scores can be entered for each question.
cases.oracle: Sections and questions render after matrix selection; entered scores are shown.

cases.title: Send the scored vendor for approval
cases.why: The PQ evaluation goes through the approval workflow before the score is generated.
cases.setup: Buyer who has completed scoring; approval workflow with an approver.
cases.steps: 1. Click **Approve** at the bottom. 2. In the **Send for Approval** side panel, add **Category** and **Location** if needed and click Next. 3. Review the approval workflow, add remarks, and select an approver. 4. Click **Continue**.
cases.expected: The vendor is submitted for approval.
cases.oracle: Send for Approval completes; the item is pending with the selected approver.

cases.title: Total Vendor Score generated after approval
cases.why: The Total Vendor Score is the PQ outcome buyers compare vendors on.
cases.setup: A scored vendor sent for approval (PRD-KBVON-050).
cases.steps: 1. Approver approves. 2. Open the vendor's profile / Onboarding Details.
cases.expected: The system generates a **Total Vendor Score** with a colour label (e.g. 95, Green - High Quality).
cases.oracle: Total Vendor Score value and colour are displayed.

cases.title: Vendor Onboarding (WF-VM-001): end-to-end order of steps
cases.why: Every vendor onboarding must pass through the same governed chain; a skipped or reordered step is a control failure.
cases.setup: Trigger: Vendor submits onboarding form. Workflow WF-VM-001 as configured in the workbook (5 steps).
cases.steps: 1. Cause the trigger: vendor submits onboarding form. 2. Let step 1 "Form Completeness Check" (System Validation, System (Auto)) complete. 3. Let step 2 "Finance Approval" (Approval, Finance Controller) complete with an approval. 4. Let step 3 "Legal / Compliance Review" (Approval, Legal / Compliance) complete with an approval. 5. Let step 4 "Category Manager Endorsement" (Approval, Category Manager) complete with an approval. 6. Let step 5 "Vendor Activation" (System Action, System (Auto)) complete.
cases.expected: The steps run in this order: 1. Form Completeness Check (System (Auto)) → 2. Finance Approval (Finance Controller) → 3. Legal / Compliance Review (Legal / Compliance) → 4. Category Manager Endorsement (Category Manager) → 5. Vendor Activation (System (Auto)). At the end: Vendor status changes to Active; SAP MDG sync triggered if integration enabled.
cases.oracle: The workflow's history shows each step, its actor and its outcome in the order above, and nothing out of sequence.

cases.title: Vendor Onboarding: step 1 "Form Completeness Check" runs automatically
cases.why: Step 1 is a System Validation step performed by System (Auto); if it does not run, everything after it rests on an unchecked premise.
cases.setup: Trigger: Vendor submits onboarding form. Condition stated for this step: All required fields and documents present.
cases.steps: 1. Cause the trigger: vendor submits onboarding form, with the condition met (all required fields and documents present). 2. Let the workflow reach step 1 "Form Completeness Check".
cases.expected: Step 1 is carried out by System (Auto) without manual action, and the workflow moves on.
cases.oracle: The workflow history records step 1 as done by System (Auto) and step 2 becomes active.

cases.title: Vendor Onboarding: step 1 "Form Completeness Check" holds when "All required fields and documents present" is not true
cases.why: The step's stated condition is "All required fields and documents present". A workflow that proceeds without it lets an incomplete item through.
cases.setup: Trigger: Vendor submits onboarding form. Condition NOT met: All required fields and documents present.
cases.steps: 1. Cause the trigger with the condition not met ("All required fields and documents present" does not hold). 2. Let the workflow reach step 1.
cases.expected: The workflow does not move past step 1 "Form Completeness Check".
cases.oracle: Step 2 never becomes active while the condition is unmet.

cases.title: Vendor Onboarding: step 2 "Finance Approval" routes to Finance Controller
cases.why: Approval 2 belongs to Finance Controller; routing it anywhere else puts the decision in the wrong hands.
cases.setup: Trigger: Vendor submits onboarding form. Approval mode: Sequential. Finance Controller user exists on the tenant.
cases.steps: 1. Cause the trigger: vendor submits onboarding form. 2. Complete the steps before step 2. 3. Check who has the pending approval.
cases.expected: The approval for step 2 "Finance Approval" is assigned to the Finance Controller, and only after the previous step has completed (sequential).
cases.oracle: The pending-approval record for step 2 names Finance Controller as the approver.

cases.title: Vendor Onboarding: step 2 "Finance Approval" is not routed before step 1 completes
cases.why: The approval mode is Sequential; an approver who sees an item before the previous level decides is approving out of order.
cases.setup: Trigger: Vendor submits onboarding form. Step 1 still pending.
cases.steps: 1. Cause the trigger. 2. Leave step 1 undecided. 3. Check the Finance Controller's pending approvals.
cases.expected: Nothing is pending for the Finance Controller at step 2 until step 1 completes.
cases.oracle: No step-2 approval record exists while step 1 is pending; it appears once that step completes.

cases.title: Vendor Onboarding: step 2 escalates to Finance Head after 48h
